\chapter{Days of the Week}
\label{ch:la-days-of-the-week}
\hlchaptermodality{5}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name all seven Roman weekdays and say which modern names kept Rome's gods and which were rewritten.}

Name the full seven-day planetary week, then sort Saturday and Sunday by which languages kept Rome's gods and which renamed them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[diēs Lūnae, Mārtis, Mercuriī, Iovis …]{diēs Lūnae to diēs Veneris — the week, before it wore down}

\label{lesson:LA-C05-dies-lunae-veneris}



\begin{quote}
Spanish says \emph{lunes}; French says \emph{lundi}. Both are worn-down descendants of something Latin still says in \textbf{full}: \textbf{diēs Lūnae}, \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{day of the Moon}.\textquotedblright{} This lesson gives you the un-eroded originals.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The five weekdays, spelled out in full}
Each weekday is simply \textbf{diēs} (\textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}) plus a \textbf{planet-god's name in the genitive} (\textquotedblleft{}of \_\_\_\textquotedblright{}):

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin} & \textbf{literally} & \textbf{planet-god} & \textbf{worn down to (Spanish / French)} \\
\midrule
\textbf{diēs Lūnae} & day of the \textbf{Moon} & Luna & lunes / lundi \\
\textbf{diēs Mārtis} & day of \textbf{Mars} & Mars & martes / mardi \\
\textbf{diēs Mercuriī} & day of \textbf{Mercury} & Mercury & miércoles / mercredi \\
\textbf{diēs Iovis} & day of \textbf{Jupiter} & Jupiter (\emph{Iuppiter}) & jueves / jeudi \\
\textbf{diēs Veneris} & day of \textbf{Venus} & Venus & viernes / vendredi \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Later languages kept only fragments of this phrase — a bare \textbf{‑s}, a bare \textbf{‑di} — but you're now looking at the whole thing, still standing.

\begin{culture}
Rome didn't always keep a seven-day planetary week. For much of the Republic, Romans ran an \textbf{eight-day market cycle} (letters \emph{A} through \emph{H}, not planets at all). The \textbf{planetary week} — the Sun, Moon, and five visible planets, each ruling a day, in a fixed order — spread into Rome later, from Hellenistic astrology, and only gradually displaced the older market cycle. So \emph{diēs Lūnae} and its siblings are themselves a Roman \textbf{adoption}, not an ancient Roman invention — a system Rome picked up and then passed on, worn down, to Spanish and French centuries later.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}diēs Lūnae\textquotedblright{} — day of the Moon — then \textquotedblleft{}diēs Mārtis,\textquotedblright{} day of Mars
  \item all five in a row — \textquotedblleft{}diēs Lūnae, Mārtis, Mercuriī, Iovis, Veneris\textquotedblright{}
  \item the wear-down — \textquotedblleft{}diēs Mārtis\textquotedblright{} became Spanish \textquotedblleft{}martes,\textquotedblright{} French \textquotedblleft{}mardi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{diēs Mārtis} literally mean, and what does it become in Spanish and French? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Day of Mars\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{martes} / \emph{mardi}.) Did Rome always use a seven-day planetary week? (\textbf{No} — for much of the Republic it ran an eight-day market cycle; the planetary week arrived later, from Hellenistic astrology.) What holds every Latin weekday name together? (\textbf{diēs} \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} + the planet-god's name in the \textbf{genitive}, \textquotedblleft{}of \_\_\_.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[diēs Saturnī, diēs Sōlis]{diēs Saturnī, diēs Sōlis — Saturday and Sunday, before the renaming}

\label{lesson:LA-C05-saturni-solis}



\begin{quote}
The Roman planetary week had \textbf{seven} days, not five. The last two — Saturn's and the Sun's — tell a story neither Spanish nor French kept: a \textbf{religious renaming} that some languages accepted, and others didn't.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The two original names}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{diēs Saturnī} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day of Saturn}.\textquotedblright{} This one survives almost untouched in English: \textbf{Saturday} (Old English \emph{Sæternesdæg}) is a \textbf{direct borrowing} of the Latin god's own name — the one weekday English kept a \textbf{Roman} god outright, rather than swapping in a Germanic equivalent, because there was no obvious Germanic god to stand in for stern old Saturn.
  \item \textbf{diēs Sōlis} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day of the Sun}.\textquotedblright{} Also a direct hit in English: \textbf{Sunday} (\emph{Sunnandæg}), a plain translation — the Sun didn't need a separate Germanic identity to be swapped in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
As Christianity spread through the Empire, Latin usage \textbf{replaced} both pagan names:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{diēs Saturnī} $\to$ \textbf{Sabbatum}, borrowing the Jewish \textbf{Sabbath} (Hebrew \emph{shabbāt}, \textquotedblleft{}to rest\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{diēs Sōlis} $\to$ \textbf{diēs Dominica}, \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{Lord's} day\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Dominus}, \textquotedblleft{}lord\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Spanish} (\emph{sábado}, \emph{domingo}) and \textbf{French} (\emph{samedi}, \emph{dimanche}) inherited these newer, \textbf{Christianized} names. \textbf{English never made the swap} — so, unexpectedly, \textbf{English's Saturday and Sunday are the older, more pagan forms}, while Spanish and French's weekend names are the \textbf{newer}, religiously rewritten ones. The direction of \textquotedblleft{}old vs. new\textquotedblright{} flips depending which language you're standing in.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}diēs Saturnī\textquotedblright{} — day of Saturn — then \textquotedblleft{}diēs Sōlis,\textquotedblright{} day of the Sun
  \item English kept these directly — \textquotedblleft{}Saturday, Sunday\textquotedblright{}
  \item Spanish/French renamed them — \textquotedblleft{}sábado/samedi (Sabbath), domingo/ dimanche (the Lord's day)\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Rome originally call Saturday and Sunday? (\textbf{Diēs Saturnī} \textquotedblleft{}day of Saturn,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{diēs Sōlis} \textquotedblleft{}day of the Sun.\textquotedblright{}) Which modern language kept these pagan names \textbf{directly}, and which two languages \textbf{renamed} them? (\textbf{English} kept them (\emph{Saturday, Sunday}); \textbf{Spanish and French} replaced them with the Christian \emph{Sabbatum} / \emph{diēs Dominica}.) So which is actually \textquotedblleft{}older\textquotedblright{} — English's weekend names, or Spanish's? (\textbf{English's} — Spanish's are the later, Christianized rewrite.)
\end{tcolorbox}
